source: NCERT Class 8 Science (Curiosity) & BHU CHS Class 9 Entrance Exam Level

questions.question: In science, a force is defined as a push or a pull on an object resulting from:
options: A single isolated object with no surroundings
An interaction between at least two objects
Only the temperature of the air
The colour of the object alone
questions.explanation: A force always comes into play only when at least two objects interact with each other (either directly or at a distance).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force, and how is its symbol correctly written?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of force is newton (written with a lowercase 'n' when spelled out) and its symbol is capital 'N'.

questions.question: What is the CGS unit of force, and how many dynes equal 1 newton (1 N)?
questions.explanation: In the CGS system, force is measured in dynes, where 1 N = 1 kg·m/s² = 1000 g × 100 cm/s² = 10⁵ dynes.

questions.question: Which of the following can a force NOT do to a physical object?
options: Change the chemical element of the atoms inside the object
Change the speed or direction of a moving object
Change the shape or size of an object
Make a stationary object start moving
questions.explanation: A force can change an object's state of motion (speed/direction) or its shape, but cannot alter its chemical identity.

questions.question: A cricketer hits a fast-approaching ball with a bat, sending it toward the boundary. Which effect of force is primarily demonstrated?
options: Change in direction and speed of motion
Zero interaction between bat and ball
questions.explanation: The push from the bat changes both the direction and speed of the moving cricket ball.

questions.question: Pressing a lump of dough with a rolling pin to make a flat chapati demonstrates which effect of force?
options: Change in the shape of an object
questions.explanation: Applying a downward push reshapes the soft dough without necessarily moving it across a long distance.

questions.question: A goalkeeper diving and catching a speeding football demonstrates that a force can:
options: Bring a moving object to rest
Increase the mass of the ball
questions.explanation: The goalkeeper applies a force opposite to the ball's motion, reducing its speed to zero.

questions.question: If an object is lying completely at rest on a horizontal table, does it mean that NO forces are acting on it?
options: No; it means friction is infinite
Yes; only moving objects experience gravity
No; forces are acting on it (such as gravity and the table's upward push), but they balance one another
Yes; gravity switches off when an object sits on a table
questions.explanation: An object remains at rest whenever all forces acting on it are balanced (net resultant force = 0 N).

questions.question: Two friends push a heavy wooden crate in the SAME direction (eastward) with forces of 35 N and 25 N respectively. What is the net force on the crate?
questions.explanation: When two forces act in the same direction on an object, the net force equals the sum of their magnitudes: 35 N + 25 N = 60 N east.

questions.question: In a game of tug-of-war, Team A pulls the rope to the left with 180 N while Team B pulls to the right with 220 N. What is the net force and direction of movement?
options: 40 N towards the right (Team B wins)
questions.explanation: When forces act in opposite directions, the net force is the difference (220 N − 180 N = 40 N) in the direction of the larger force (right).

questions.question: If two teams pull a tug-of-war rope in opposite directions with an equal force of 150 N each, the rope does not move because:
options: The net force is zero (balanced forces)
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite forces (150 N − 150 N = 0 N) are balanced forces and produce no change in the state of motion.

questions.question: What two quantities are required to completely specify a force (making force a vector quantity)?
questions.explanation: A force's effect depends on both how strong it is (magnitude) and which way it acts (direction).

questions.question: When you push a heavy wall with your hand, what happens to your hand at the exact same moment?
options: The wall pulls your hand forward
The wall exerts an equal and opposite push back on your hand until you stop pushing
Your hand experiences no force at all
Gravity stops acting on your hand
questions.explanation: Forces always occur in interaction pairs: whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts a force back on A as long as the interaction lasts.

questions.question: Is a net force definitely acting on a car that is moving in a non-uniform motion (speeding up, slowing down, or turning a curve)?
options: Yes, because any change in speed or direction of motion requires an unbalanced force
No, turning a corner requires zero force
Only if the car is driving uphill
No, force is only needed to start a car from rest
questions.explanation: Non-uniform motion means velocity (speed and/or direction) is changing, which can only happen under a non-zero net force.

questions.question: Turning the handlebar of a moving bicycle to avoid a puddle is an example of force changing the object's:
questions.explanation: Steering applies a force that alters the bicycle's direction of travel.

questions.question: Why does cycling against a strong headwind feel much harder than cycling on a calm day?
options: The blowing wind exerts an opposing push (force) against the cyclist and bicycle
Gravity becomes twice as strong in wind
Wind increases the mass of the bicycle frame
questions.explanation: Moving air pushes backwards against the cyclist, so the cyclist must apply a greater forward muscular force on the pedals.

questions.question: Why does a bicycle speed up rapidly while coasting downhill even when you stop pedalling?
options: Friction pushes the bicycle faster downhill
The Earth's gravitational force pulls the bicycle and rider downhill along the slope
Magnetic force from the road pulls the rubber tyres
questions.explanation: A component of gravity pulls objects downward along an inclined slope, increasing their speed automatically.

questions.question: Opening a desk drawer toward yourself is an example of:
questions.explanation: Drawing an object closer to yourself applies a pulling force.

questions.question: What happens to the speed of a rolling ball if you gently push it in the SAME direction in which it is already moving?
questions.explanation: A force applied along the direction of motion accelerates the object, increasing its speed.

questions.question: What happens to a moving object if a force is applied in the direction OPPOSITE to its motion?
options: Its speed decreases, and it may eventually stop or reverse direction
questions.explanation: An opposing force (like brakes or friction) decelerates a moving object.

questions.question: A force of 12 N acts northward and a force of 12 N acts southward on a stationary block simultaneously. What happens to the block?
options: It remains at rest because the two forces cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Equal forces acting along the same line in opposite directions yield a net force of 0 N.

questions.question: Stretching a rubber band with both hands is an example of a force causing:
questions.explanation: Pulling both ends of a rubber band elongates it, demonstrating deformation (change in shape).

questions.question: What is meant by the 'state of motion' of an object in physics?
options: Only whether it is solid, liquid, or gas
Both its speed and its direction of motion (including being at rest, where speed is zero)
questions.explanation: An object's state of motion is described by its speed and direction; zero speed represents the state of rest.

questions.question: Can balanced forces ever change the shape of a soft object like a rubber ball or a sponge?
options: Only if the ball is made of iron
Yes — pressing a rubber ball equally from both opposite sides balances the net force to zero yet squeezes its shape
No — balanced forces can never affect an object in any way
questions.explanation: While balanced forces cannot change an object's state of motion (velocity), opposing pushes or pulls can compress or stretch its shape!

questions.question: Which of the following actions involves BOTH a push and a pull simultaneously in everyday life?
options: A magnet attracting an iron pin from a distance
Sawing a wooden plank back and forth (or rowing a boat / playing a violin)
An apple falling freely from a tree
questions.explanation: Sawing alternates pushing forward and pulling back through direct muscular contact.

questions.question: Forces that act only when two objects are physically touching each other (directly or through a rope/stick) are called:
questions.explanation: Contact forces — such as muscular force and frictional force — require physical contact between interacting bodies.

questions.question: Which pair consists ONLY of contact forces?
questions.explanation: Muscular force and friction require physical contact; magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces act at a distance.

questions.question: Which force enables bullocks to plough a field, horses to pull a cart, and humans to lift a school bag?
questions.explanation: Muscular force is generated by the contraction and relaxation of muscles in living beings.

questions.question: Which vital internal processes inside the human body depend continuously on muscular force?
options: Pumping of blood by the heart and pushing food down the alimentary canal during digestion
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscles contract rhythmically to circulate blood, and smooth muscles in the food pipe push food along (peristalsis).

questions.question: A ball rolling on a flat playground slows down and eventually stops on its own because of:
options: The force of friction acting opposite to its motion
An increase in the ball's weight
questions.explanation: Friction between the rolling ball and the ground opposes its motion and gradually brings it to rest.

questions.question: In which direction does the force of friction ALWAYS act?
options: Opposite to the direction of motion (or intended motion) of the object
Always toward the Geographic North Pole
In the same direction as the object's motion
questions.explanation: Friction opposes relative sliding or rolling between two surfaces in contact.

questions.question: What is the microscopic cause of friction between two solid surfaces in contact?
options: Air bubbles trapped inside solid iron
Interlocking of tiny microscopic irregularities (bumps and grooves) present on both surfaces
questions.explanation: Even surfaces that look mirror-smooth have microscopic irregularities; when pressed together, these ridges interlock and resist movement.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Cause of Friction

questions.question: If you push the same wooden block with equal effort across four surfaces — polished glass, smooth tile, rough wood, and loose sand — on which surface will it travel the FARTHEST before stopping?
questions.explanation: Polished glass has the smallest surface irregularities and therefore offers the least friction, letting the block slide the farthest.

questions.question: Why is it much easier to slip and fall on a wet bathroom floor or soapy tile?
options: Water or soap fills surface irregularities and forms a thin layer that sharply reduces friction between feet and floor
questions.explanation: Walking requires friction to push backward against the ground; water/soap acts as a lubricant, reducing grip.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Application • Friction in Daily Life

questions.question: What is the special name given to the frictional force exerted by fluids (liquids and gases such as water and air)?
questions.explanation: Air, water, and other fluids exert a resistive frictional force called drag on objects moving through them.

questions.question: Why are aeroplanes, bullet trains, ships, birds, and fish designed with sleek, tapered 'streamlined' shapes?
options: To increase air resistance as much as possible
To make them heavier than water
To store static electricity on their wings
To minimize fluid friction (air or water drag) and save energy while moving fast
questions.explanation: A streamlined shape allows air or water to flow smoothly around the body, drastically cutting drag.

questions.question: Arrange the three types of solid friction — Static friction, Sliding friction, and Rolling friction — in DECREASING order of magnitude:
options: Rolling friction > Sliding friction > Static friction
Sliding friction > Static friction > Rolling friction
All three are always strictly equal
Static friction > Sliding friction > Rolling friction
questions.explanation: It takes the most force to overcome static interlocking at rest, slightly less to keep sliding, and far less when rolling on wheels.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Types of Friction

questions.question: Why are heavy travel suitcases fitted with small wheels at the bottom?
options: Because wheels reduce the mass of clothes inside
Because rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, making them easy to pull
Because wheels increase friction against the floor
questions.explanation: Replacing sliding with rolling drastically cuts friction, reducing the muscular effort needed.

questions.question: Why do mechanics place steel ball bearings inside bicycle wheel hubs and electric ceiling fans?
options: To convert sliding friction into much smaller rolling friction and reduce wear and tear
To make the wheel stop faster
questions.explanation: Ball bearings roll smoothly between moving metal parts, lowering friction, heat loss, and mechanical wear.

questions.question: Why do carrom players sprinkle fine talcum/boric powder on a carrom board before playing?
options: To increase friction and stop the coins
To increase the weight of the striker
To fill tiny surface irregularities and reduce friction so the striker glides smoothly
To stick the coins firmly to the wood
questions.explanation: Fine dry powder acts as a dry lubricant between the wooden board and the carrom coins.

questions.question: Why do car tyres and sports shoes have deep grooves (treads) carved into their rubber soles?
options: To increase friction and provide a firm grip on roads, preventing skidding
To reduce air pressure inside the tyre
To reduce friction so the vehicle slides freely
To make the tyres completely smooth
questions.explanation: Treads channel away water and increase interlocking grip with the road for safe braking and running.

questions.question: Why do kabaddi players rub dry soil or chalk powder on their hands before a match?
options: To reduce friction so opponents slip away
To increase friction for a firmer, non-slip grip on their opponents
questions.explanation: Dry soil absorbs sweat and roughens the palm surface, boosting friction and grip.

questions.question: Why is friction often called a 'necessary evil'?
options: Because it only acts on iron objects
Because it only exists on rainy days
It is essential for walking, writing, and braking, yet it also causes wear and tear of machinery and wastes energy as heat
questions.explanation: Without friction we couldn't walk, hold a pen, or stop a car — yet friction also wears out shoe soles, tyres, and engine parts while generating unwanted heat.

questions.question: What happens when you rub your palms together vigorously on a cold winter morning?
options: Magnetic poles form on your fingers
Friction between the palms converts mechanical energy into heat, warming your hands
questions.explanation: Work done against friction produces heat energy — the same principle lights a matchstick when struck against a rough box!

questions.question: Which factor does the force of friction between two solid surfaces depend upon?
options: Both the roughness/nature of the surfaces and how hard the two surfaces are pressed together (normal force)
Only the colour of the surfaces
questions.explanation: Rougher surfaces and heavier objects (which press surfaces harder together) produce greater interlocking and higher friction.

questions.question: Applying oil or grease to the hinges of a creaking door helps because oil acts as a:
options: Lubricant that reduces friction between the metal parts
questions.explanation: Lubricants form a thin slippery film separating metal surfaces, cutting friction and noise.

questions.question: Why do gymnasts apply coarse chalk powder on their hands before performing on horizontal bars?
options: To make their hands as slippery as possible
To absorb moisture and increase friction for a secure grip
questions.explanation: Chalk keeps palms dry and rough, preventing dangerous slips during athletic routines.

questions.question: Why do meteors (shooting stars) burn up brightly upon entering the Earth's atmosphere?
options: Cold air freezes them until they glow
Intense air friction (drag) at extreme speed generates tremendous heat that vaporizes the meteor
Earth's magnetic poles melt them directly
questions.explanation: High-speed friction against atmospheric air molecules heats space rocks to thousands of degrees Celsius.

questions.question: A ball rolls down a smooth ramp onto a horizontal floor and stops at point A. How could you make the SAME ball travel PAST point A before stopping?
options: Blow a strong fan directly against the ball
Replace the ball with a rough cube
Make the horizontal floor smoother (e.g., polished glass or oiled surface) to reduce friction
Spread rough sand or a thick carpet on the floor
questions.explanation: Lowering friction on the horizontal track allows the ball to retain its speed longer and roll beyond point A.

questions.question: Using a wooden stick to push a floating ball out of a puddle is an example of:
questions.explanation: Contact forces can be direct (hand touching object) or indirect (through a stick, rope, or bat).

questions.question: Forces that can act on an object from a distance without any physical contact are called:
questions.explanation: Magnetic force, electrostatic force, and gravitational force are the three major non-contact forces studied in Class 8.

questions.question: Which of the following groups contains ONLY non-contact forces?
options: Magnetic force, Electrostatic force, Gravitational force
questions.explanation: Magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces all act across empty space without physical touching.

questions.question: What happens when the North pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the North pole of another bar magnet?
options: They cancel each other's magnetism permanently
questions.explanation: Like magnetic poles (North–North or South–South) repel each other, whereas unlike poles (North–South) attract.

questions.question: If two ring magnets are slipped onto a vertical wooden stick with their LIKE poles facing each other, why does the upper magnet float in mid-air?
options: Friction from the wooden stick lifts it up
Upward magnetic repulsion between the like poles balances the downward pull of gravity on the upper magnet
Air pressure glues the magnet to the stick
Gravity does not act on magnets
questions.explanation: Magnetic repulsion acts without physical contact, holding the top ring magnet suspended in equilibrium.

questions.question: Which set of metals consists exclusively of magnetic materials strongly attracted by a magnet?
questions.explanation: Iron, nickel, cobalt (and steel alloys) are ferromagnetic materials attracted by magnets.

questions.question: A freely suspended magnetic compass needle always points toward Geographic North–South because of:
options: Magnetic force exerted by the Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: Earth behaves like a giant bar magnet, aligning compass needles along the magnetic North–South direction.

questions.question: What is the surest test to confirm whether a given metal bar is a true magnet (and not merely an unmagnetized iron bar)?
options: Measuring its mass on a balance
Checking if it sinks in water
questions.explanation: An unmagnetized iron bar is attracted by BOTH poles of a magnet, whereas only another magnet can be REPELLED by a like pole.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Sure Test of Magnetism

questions.question: When a dry plastic scale or comb is rubbed vigorously with polythene or dry hair and brought near tiny bits of paper, the paper bits jump up and stick to it due to:
questions.explanation: Rubbing builds static electrical charges on the plastic, which then exerts an electrostatic pull on uncharged paper bits without touching them.

questions.question: Why are the electrical charges produced on a plastic scale or balloon by rubbing called 'static charges'?
options: Because they remain stationary on the surface and do not flow by themselves like an electric current
Because they move at the speed of sound
Because they only appear inside steel wires
questions.explanation: Static charges stay localized on insulating surfaces until discharged; when charges move through a circuit, they form an electric current.

questions.question: Two inflated balloons are both rubbed with the same woollen cloth and hung close to each other by threads. What will you observe?
options: The two balloons move away from (repel) each other because both acquired the same kind of static charge
The two balloons stick tightly together
Nothing happens because rubber cannot be charged
questions.explanation: Rubbing both balloons identically with wool gives them like charges, and like charges repel each other.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Like Charges Repel

questions.question: If you bring the woollen cloth (that was just used to rub a balloon) close to the rubbed balloon, what happens?
options: The balloon and the woollen cloth attract each other because they acquired opposite charges
The cloth turns into a magnet
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons between materials, leaving the rubbing object and the rubbed object with opposite (unlike) charges, which attract.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Unlike Charges Attract

questions.question: What are the two kinds of electrical charges found in nature?
questions.explanation: All static electrical phenomena arise from positive and negative charges: like charges repel, unlike charges attract.

questions.question: Why should you NOT touch the rubbed part of a charged plastic straw or balloon with your bare hand or a metal rod during an electrostatic demonstration?
options: It will melt the plastic instantly
It will turn the plastic into iron
Your body or the metal conducts the static charge away to the ground (earthing), discharging the object
questions.explanation: Human skin and metals are conductors; touching the charged area lets static charges leak away to Earth.

questions.question: What is the name of the simple scientific instrument used to detect whether an object carries an electrical charge?
questions.explanation: An electroscope (made with a metal wire and thin aluminium or gold leaves inside a jar) detects static charge when its two foil leaves diverge due to like-charge repulsion.

questions.question: In a simple homemade electroscope with two hanging strips of aluminium foil, why do the two foil strips spread apart when a charged rod touches the top copper wire?
options: Both aluminium strips receive the same type of charge and therefore repel each other
The strips become oppositely charged and repel
Magnetic poles form on the glass jar
questions.explanation: Charge conducts down the copper wire equally to both foil leaves; because like charges repel, the leaves diverge.

questions.question: What is formed when electrical charges are NOT static, but instead move continuously through a closed conducting circuit?
questions.explanation: Flowing electric charges constitute an electric current, which powers lamps and produces heating and magnetic effects.

questions.question: Why do you sometimes hear tiny crackling sounds and see faint sparks when taking off a woollen or synthetic sweater in dry winter darkness?
options: Woollen fibres are burning due to gravity
Magnets inside the sweater are clashing
Static electrical charges built up by friction between clothes discharge through the air
Water vapour is boiling on the skin
questions.explanation: Rubbing dry synthetic or woollen fabrics transfers static charges; rapid discharge creates tiny sparks and crackles.

questions.question: Can a charged body exert an electrostatic force on an UNCHARGED neutral object (like small dry paper pieces)?
options: Only if the uncharged body is made of iron
No — electrostatic force acts only if both bodies are already charged
Yes — a charged body can attract both an oppositely charged body and an uncharged light body
questions.explanation: A charged object induces slight opposite charge separation on the near side of an uncharged insulator like paper, pulling it in.

questions.question: How is an electromagnet similar to a permanent bar magnet?
options: Both work only with wooden cores
Both exert a non-contact magnetic force (attraction and repulsion) when active
questions.explanation: When electric current flows through a coil around a soft iron core, the electromagnet behaves like a magnet and exerts non-contact magnetic force.

questions.question: Which property is shared by BOTH magnetic force and electrostatic force, but NOT by gravitational force?
options: Both act only on the Moon
Both depend solely on an object's colour
Both can be either attractive OR repulsive, whereas gravitational force is ALWAYS attractive
questions.explanation: Gravity only pulls masses together; magnets and electric charges can both attract (unlike) and repel (like).

questions.question: Why do electrostatic experiments (like attracting paper bits with a rubbed comb) work much better on a dry winter day than on a humid rainy day?
options: Plastic combs lose their mass in summer
Humid air contains moisture that lets static charges leak away quickly, whereas dry air insulates them well
questions.explanation: Moisture on surfaces conducts static charge away into the air and ground, preventing charge build-up.

questions.question: Which natural atmospheric phenomenon is a giant electrostatic discharge caused by charge build-up between clouds or between a cloud and the ground?
questions.explanation: Rubbing of ice crystals and water droplets inside thunderclouds creates massive static charge separation, releasing huge lightning sparks.

questions.question: A crane in a scrapyard lifts heavy iron scrap from a pile without tying any ropes to it by using:
questions.explanation: Scrapyard cranes switch on giant electromagnets to attract iron scrap and switch off the current to drop it.

questions.question: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, by convention what kind of charge does the glass rod acquire?
options: Positive charge (and the silk cloth acquires an equal negative charge)
Negative charge (and silk acquires zero charge)
questions.explanation: By standard physics convention, rubbing glass with silk leaves the glass rod positively charged and the silk negatively charged.

questions.question: If two charged objects are placed a small distance apart in dry air, is there a force acting between them?
options: Yes — an electrostatic force acts between them even without touching
No — they must be glued together to exert force
Only if they are placed inside water
Only if they are made of steel
questions.explanation: Electrostatic force is a non-contact force that operates across the air gap separating charged objects.

questions.question: Why do ripe fruits from trees, raindrops from clouds, and a stone dropped from a roof all fall straight down toward the Earth?
options: Because of the Earth's gravitational force (gravity) pulling every object toward its centre
questions.explanation: Gravity is the non-contact attractive force with which the Earth pulls all objects toward itself.

questions.question: Gravitational force is ALWAYS:
questions.explanation: Unlike magnetic or electrostatic forces, gravity never repels — it always pulls objects toward each other.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Nature of Gravity

questions.question: When you throw a cricket ball vertically straight upward, what happens to its speed as it rises?
options: Its speed steadily decreases until it stops momentarily at the highest point
Its speed steadily increases until it reaches space
questions.explanation: Earth's gravity pulls downward opposite to the ball's upward velocity, decelerating it to zero speed at the peak.

questions.question: When a ball thrown vertically upward reaches its exact HIGHEST point and momentarily stops, what is the direction of the gravitational force acting on it?
options: Zero — gravity disappears at the topmost point
Vertically downward (gravity continues to pull it toward the Earth)
questions.explanation: Even though the ball's instantaneous speed is zero at the peak, Earth's gravity NEVER turns off — it continues pulling downward, causing the ball to fall back!
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Topmost Point Trap

questions.question: During the downward fall of a stone dropped from a building, what happens to its speed as it approaches the ground?
options: Its speed continuously increases because gravity pulls in the same direction as its motion
questions.explanation: Since gravity acts downward along the direction of fall, the falling stone accelerates.

questions.question: Which scientist formulated the Universal Law of Gravitation after investigating why apples fall downward and how the Moon orbits the Earth?
questions.explanation: Sir Isaac Newton showed that the same universal gravitational force pulls an apple to the ground and keeps planets and moons in orbit.

questions.question: Does gravitational attraction exist ONLY between the Earth and objects on Earth, or between ALL objects with mass in the universe?
options: Only the Earth has gravity; the Moon and Sun have none
Only planets have gravity; stars do not
Every object with mass in the universe attracts every other object with mass
questions.explanation: Gravity is universal — even two books on a desk attract each other, though the force is too tiny to notice compared to Earth's huge mass.

questions.question: Which force keeps the Moon revolving in orbit around the Earth and the Earth revolving around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The mutual gravitational pull between celestial bodies holds moons around planets and planets around the Sun.

questions.question: What is the approximate value of acceleration due to gravity (g) near the Earth's surface?
options: 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10 m/s² in school calculations)
questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface, freely falling objects accelerate downward at roughly 9.8 m/s² (~10 m/s²).

questions.question: Why does a ball thrown vertically upward fall back along a straight vertical line rather than curving sideways (ignoring wind)?
options: Because the Earth's gravitational pull acts strictly vertically downward toward Earth's centre
Because the ball has zero mass
Because air friction pushes it upward
questions.explanation: Motion strictly under vertical gravitational pull follows a straight vertical path up and down.

questions.question: If a heavy iron ball and a light feather are dropped from the exact same height inside a completely airless VACUUM tube, which reaches the bottom first?
options: The iron ball reaches 10 times faster
Neither falls because gravity needs air
The feather floats to the ceiling
Both reach the bottom at the exact same time
questions.explanation: In a vacuum (zero air resistance), all objects accelerate downward at the exact same rate g regardless of their mass! (Demonstrated by Galileo and on the Moon by Apollo 15.)
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Free Fall in Vacuum

questions.question: In normal open air, why does a flat sheet of paper fall much more slowly than a crumpled ball made from an identical sheet of paper?
options: Flat paper is repelled by Earth's magnetism
The flat sheet has a larger surface area and faces much greater upward air resistance (drag)
The crumpled ball has more mass
questions.explanation: Both have identical mass and weight, but the flat sheet experiences much larger air drag slowing its descent.

questions.question: Why does a river always flow downhill from high mountains toward the sea?
options: Earth's gravitational force pulls water continuously from higher elevation to lower elevation
questions.explanation: Gravity drives the downward flow of all rivers, waterfalls, and glacial meltwater.

questions.question: Why do we feel slightly 'light' or floating for a brief instant right as a playground swing reaches its highest point and starts coming back down?
options: Because your mass drops to zero
Because Earth's gravity vanishes completely on swings
Because at the turnaround peak your body momentarily begins accelerating downward under gravity, reducing the upward push felt from the seat
questions.explanation: During rapid downward acceleration, the normal contact force from the seat decreases briefly, creating a light 'floating' sensation.

questions.question: Which force holds the blanket of air (Earth's atmosphere) tightly around our planet instead of letting gases escape into space?
options: Magnetic force of the North Pole
questions.explanation: Earth's strong gravity keeps atmospheric gases bound to the planet; smaller bodies like the Moon lack enough gravity to hold an atmosphere.

questions.question: Which force is responsible for high and low tides in Earth's oceans?
options: Gravitational pull of the Moon (and the Sun) on Earth's ocean water
questions.explanation: The Moon's gravitational attraction creates tidal bulges in Earth's oceans as Earth rotates.

questions.question: When a ball is rising upward after being tossed, which two forces act on it (in open air), and in which direction?
options: Both gravity AND air resistance act downward, opposing the ball's upward motion
Gravity acts upward and air resistance acts downward
questions.explanation: Gravity always pulls down, and air drag always opposes the current direction of motion (so drag also acts downward while the ball rises).

questions.question: When the same ball is falling back downward through open air, what are the directions of gravity and air resistance?
options: Neither force acts during a fall
Gravity acts downward, while air resistance acts upward (opposing the fall)
Gravity acts upward and air resistance acts downward
Both gravity and air resistance act downward
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls downward, while fluid friction (air drag) opposes the downward fall by pushing upward.

questions.question: Why is it much harder to pedal a bicycle uphill than on a flat road?
options: You have to overcome a backward component of Earth's gravitational pull in addition to friction
questions.explanation: Going uphill means lifting your own weight and the bicycle against gravity.

questions.question: Why does the gravitational force of the Moon pull objects with only about one-sixth (1/6) the strength of Earth's gravity?
options: Because the Moon has much less mass than the Earth
Because the Moon is made of plastic
Because the Moon has no water
Because the Moon does not rotate
questions.explanation: Gravitational pull depends on the mass and radius of the celestial body; the Moon's much smaller mass produces ~1/6th of Earth's surface gravity.

questions.question: If an astronaut jumps with the same muscular effort on the Moon as on Earth, what happens?
options: The astronaut jumps roughly 6 times higher on the Moon due to weaker lunar gravity
The astronaut jumps lower than on Earth
The astronaut cannot lift off the ground at all
questions.explanation: With only ~1/6th of Earth's downward gravitational pull, the same upward push launches the astronaut much higher.

questions.question: If you drop a stone from a bridge into a river, which force makes the stone fall through the air before hitting the water?
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the unsupported stone straight downward toward the river surface.

questions.question: How does the gravitational attraction between two objects change if the distance between them increases?
options: Gravity turns repulsive at large distances
The gravitational force decreases as distance increases
Distance has zero effect on gravity
questions.explanation: Gravitational force weakens with increasing separation (following the inverse-square law).

questions.question: Why do paratroopers open a wide parachute while jumping from an aeroplane?
options: To generate magnetic repulsion from the ground
To drastically increase upward air resistance (drag) so it balances gravity and slows their fall to a safe landing speed
To increase the downward gravitational force
questions.explanation: A wide canopy traps huge amounts of air, creating strong upward drag that prevents dangerous high-speed impact.

questions.question: Where on Earth's surface is the gravitational pull (and therefore an object's weight) slightly GREATER?
options: High on top of Mount Everest
Exactly identical to 10 decimal places everywhere
At the Poles (slightly greater than at the Equator because the Earth is flattened at the poles, placing them closer to Earth's centre)
questions.explanation: Since Earth is an oblate spheroid, the polar radius is slightly smaller than the equatorial radius, making gravity marginally stronger at the poles.

questions.question: What is the scientific definition of the 'weight' of an object?
options: The number of atoms in an object measured in kilograms
The surface area of an object
The total volume of space an object occupies
The gravitational force with which the Earth (or another planet) pulls the object toward itself
questions.explanation: Weight is a force (gravitational pull on a mass), whereas mass is the amount of matter inside the object.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Mass vs Weight

questions.question: What is the SI unit of WEIGHT?
questions.explanation: Because weight is a gravitational force, its SI unit is newton (N) — NOT kilogram!
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • SI Units Trap

questions.question: What is the SI unit of MASS?
questions.explanation: Mass measures the amount of matter in a body and its SI unit is the kilogram (kg).

questions.question: Which simple laboratory device uses the stretching of a coiled spring to directly measure the WEIGHT (force) of an object?
questions.explanation: When an object hangs from a spring balance hook, Earth's gravitational pull stretches the spring proportionally to the object's weight in newtons.

questions.question: Which instrument compares an unknown mass against standard known masses and gives the exact same reading on both Earth and the Moon?
questions.explanation: In a beam balance, gravity pulls equally on both pans, so a 1 kg mass balances a 1 kg standard on the Moon just as it does on Earth.
questions.ncertRef: CHS High-Yield • Beam vs Spring Balance

questions.question: If an astronaut carries a rock of mass 6 kg from Earth to the Moon, what will be the MASS of the rock on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and NEVER changes with location; only weight changes with gravity!

questions.question: An object weighs 60 N on Earth. Since lunar gravity is about 1/6th of Earth's gravity, what will its approximate WEIGHT be on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Weight on Moon ≈ (1/6) × Weight on Earth = 60 N ÷ 6 = 10 N.

questions.question: On Earth, an object of mass 1 kg has a weight of approximately 10 N. What is the approximate weight of a 1 kg object on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Due to the Moon's weaker gravity (g ≈ 1.6 m/s²), a 1 kg mass weighs about 1.6 N on the Moon.

questions.question: If a 1 kg object weighs about 10 N on Earth, on which planet will the SAME 1 kg object weigh the MOST (~25.4 N)?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the most massive planet in our solar system; its strong gravity makes a 1 kg object weigh about 25.4 N!

questions.question: A 1 kg object weighs about 10 N on Earth. What is its approximate weight on Mars?
questions.explanation: Mars has lower gravity than Earth (~3.8 m/s²), so a 1 kg mass weighs roughly 3.8 N on Mars.

questions.question: A 1 kg object weighs about 10 N on Earth. What is its approximate weight on Venus?
questions.explanation: Venus is close in size and mass to Earth, so a 1 kg mass weighs about 9 N on Venus.

questions.question: A spring balance has major markings at 0 N, 1 N, 2 N ... up to 10 N, with 5 equal small divisions between 0 N and 1 N. What is the smallest weight (least count) it can measure?
questions.explanation: Least count = (Difference between two big marks) ÷ (Number of small divisions) = 1 N ÷ 5 = 0.2 N.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Numerical • Spring Balance Least Count

questions.question: A spring balance has major marks every 2 N and 10 equal small divisions between 0 N and 2 N. What is its least count?
questions.explanation: Least count = 2 N ÷ 10 = 0.2 N per small division.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Numerical • Spring Balance Least Count

questions.question: What could happen if you hang a 25 N iron block from a spring balance whose maximum range is only 0 to 10 N?
options: It will measure mass in litres
The spring will turn into a magnet
The spring may overstretch permanently and damage the spring balance
It will automatically convert 25 N into 5 N
questions.explanation: Never exceed an instrument's maximum range, as overstretching destroys the spring's elasticity.

questions.question: In everyday shopping, people often say 'the weight of this wheat bag is 10 kg'. Why is this statement scientifically inaccurate?
options: Because 10 kg is the MASS of the wheat bag, whereas its weight should be expressed in newtons (about 98 N or 100 N)
Because kilograms are used only for liquids
questions.explanation: In science, mass is stated in kg/g and weight (gravitational force) is stated in newtons (N).
questions.ncertRef: CHS Conceptual • Everyday vs Scientific Terms

questions.question: What is the approximate weight on Earth of a school bag whose mass is 5 kg? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Weight W = mass × g = 5 kg × 10 m/s² = 50 N.

questions.question: If an object weighs 45 N on Earth (taking g = 10 m/s²), what is its mass?
questions.explanation: Mass m = W ÷ g = 45 N ÷ 10 m/s² = 4.5 kg.

questions.question: A stone has a mass of 2 kg. What will be its approximate weight on Jupiter (where a 1 kg mass weighs 25.4 N)?
questions.explanation: On Jupiter, weight = 2 × 25.4 N = 50.8 N, while its mass remains 2 kg.

questions.question: An astronaut's backpack has a mass of 10 kg. What is its approximate weight on the Moon (where 1 kg weighs 1.6 N)?
questions.explanation: On the Moon, weight = 10 × 1.6 N = 16 N (while its mass stays 10 kg).

questions.question: Why do some laboratory spring balances display BOTH a newton (N) scale and a gram (g) scale side by side?
options: Because on Earth's surface, weight is nearly proportional to mass, allowing indirect mass reading on Earth
Because spring balances do not use gravity
Because grams and newtons are identical everywhere in space
questions.explanation: The gram markings on a spring balance are calibrated assuming Earth's gravity; on another planet, the gram scale would read incorrectly!

questions.question: Can the weight of an object ever become ZERO (weightlessness), even though its mass is NOT zero?
options: No — weight can never be zero if mass is non-zero
Yes — in deep outer space far from any planet or star (where gravitational pull is negligible)
questions.explanation: Mass is never zero for any matter, but weight (W = mg) becomes zero wherever gravitational pull g is zero.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly contrasts MASS and WEIGHT?
options: Mass is measured in newtons; Weight is measured in kilograms
Weight stays constant on all planets; Mass changes
Both mass and weight are zero on the Moon
Mass is scalar and constant everywhere; Weight is a force (vector) that varies with gravity
questions.explanation: Mass depends only on the matter inside a body; weight depends on local gravitational pull and acts downward.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Mass vs Weight

questions.question: When you hang a heavier stone from a spring compared to a light pencil box, what happens to the stretch of the spring?
options: The stretch is identical for all objects
The spring stretches MORE because Earth pulls the heavier stone with a greater gravitational force
questions.explanation: Greater weight produces greater downward pull, stretching the coiled spring further.

questions.question: A boy weighs 480 N on Earth. If he travels to Mars (where gravity is 0.38 times Earth's gravity), what will his weight on Mars be?
questions.explanation: Weight on Mars = 480 N × 0.38 = 182.4 N.

questions.question: Which quantity can NEVER be zero for a real physical object?
questions.explanation: Every physical object contains matter, so its mass is always positive and non-zero.

questions.question: What is the upward force exerted by a liquid (such as water) on any object immersed in it called?
questions.explanation: All liquids (and gases) push upward on immersed objects; this upward force is called upthrust or buoyant force.

questions.question: Why does a plastic mug filled with water feel noticeably LIGHTER while it is still submerged inside a bucket of water, and heavier as soon as you lift it out?
options: Because the mug loses plastic underwater
Because water destroys gravity inside a bucket
Because air pushes the mug downward harder than water
Because the surrounding water exerts an upward buoyant force (upthrust) on the mug while it is submerged
questions.explanation: Upthrust supports part of the mug's weight underwater, reducing the upward muscular force your hand needs to apply.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Upthrust in Daily Life

questions.question: If you push a tightly closed empty plastic bottle deep into a bucket of water and release it, why does it immediately bounce back to the surface?
options: Because the upward buoyant force of water is greater than the downward gravitational pull (weight) on the empty bottle
Because gravity pushes empty bottles upward
questions.explanation: When upward buoyant force exceeds the object's weight, the net force is upward, pushing the bottle to the surface.

questions.question: When an object is placed in water, under what condition will it SINK to the bottom?
options: When buoyant force is greater than the object's weight
When buoyant force equals the object's weight
When the downward gravitational force (weight of the object) is GREATER than the maximum upward buoyant force
questions.explanation: If downward weight > upward upthrust, the net force points downward and the object sinks.

questions.question: Under what condition does an object FLOAT steadily on the surface of a liquid?
options: When the upward buoyant force equals the downward weight of the object
When the weight is 10 times larger than buoyant force
Only when the water is boiling
questions.explanation: A floating object sinks just deep enough so that the upward buoyant force exactly balances its downward weight.

questions.question: Which famous ancient Greek scientist discovered that an object fully or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the WEIGHT OF THE FLUID IT DISPLACES?
questions.explanation: This fundamental law of hydrostatics is known as Archimedes' Principle.

questions.question: According to Archimedes' Principle, an object floats in a liquid when the weight of the liquid displaced by it is:
options: Equal to the weight of the object
Less than half the weight of the object
Equal to the mass of the bucket
questions.explanation: If the maximum displaced liquid weighs less than the object, it sinks; if it can displace liquid equal to its own weight, it floats.

questions.question: Why does a tiny metal coin sink immediately in a glass of water, whereas a much heavier wooden block floats?
options: Because metal coins are attracted to Earth's magnetic core
Because water has no upthrust on small objects
The dense metal coin displaces water weighing less than itself, while the less-dense wooden block displaces enough water to balance its weight
questions.explanation: Floating depends on density (and displaced water weight), not simply on total weight — metal is denser than water, whereas wood is less dense.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Coin vs Wood

questions.question: Why does a solid iron nail sink in water, whereas a massive ship made of thousands of tonnes of iron floats easily on the ocean?
options: The ship's hollow hull encloses a huge volume of air, making its average density less than water so it displaces water equal to its huge weight
Because ocean water has no gravity
Because ships are coated with magnets
Because iron becomes lighter near coasts
questions.explanation: By shaping iron into a wide hollow hull, the ship displaces an enormous volume of water whose weight matches the ship's weight.
questions.ncertRef: CHS Exam Favorite • Why Ships Float

questions.question: Which natural volcanic rock is famous for FLOATING on water instead of sinking?
questions.explanation: When gas-rich volcanic lava cools rapidly, it traps countless tiny air bubbles inside, forming porous, low-density Pumice rock that floats on water!

questions.question: How does the density of a liquid affect the buoyant force it exerts on an immersed object?
options: Liquid density has zero effect on buoyancy
Only pure distilled water exerts buoyant force
A denser liquid exerts LESS buoyant force
A denser liquid (like salty seawater) exerts a GREATER buoyant force than a less dense liquid (like freshwater)
questions.explanation: Since displaced saltwater weighs more per unit volume than freshwater, swimmers and ships float higher in the sea (and effortlessly in the Dead Sea!).

questions.question: Three blocks of identical size and shape (Block 1, Block 2, Block 3) float in water: Block 2 dips deepest, Block 3 dips to medium depth, and Block 1 dips shallowest. Which order of their weights (w₁, w₂, w₃) is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: A heavier floating block must sink deeper to displace more water so that upward buoyant force equals its larger weight. Hence deeper dip = greater weight: w₂ > w₃ > w₁!

questions.question: A stone weighs 12 N in air. When completely immersed in water, a spring balance reads 8 N. What is the buoyant force exerted by the water on the stone?
questions.explanation: Apparent loss in weight = Buoyant force = Weight in air − Weight in water = 12 N − 8 N = 4 N.

questions.question: If an object floating in freshwater is moved into dense salty seawater, what happens to the submerged part of the object?
options: It rises slightly higher (less of it stays submerged) because seawater provides greater upthrust per unit volume
It sinks completely to the bottom
It submerges deeper than in freshwater
questions.explanation: Higher density of saltwater means the object needs to displace a smaller volume of water to balance its weight.

questions.question: Which instrument based on Archimedes' Principle is used to test the purity (density) of milk?
questions.explanation: A lactometer floats at different depths depending on milk density, directly applying Archimedes' Principle.

questions.question: Why does a submarine take water into its special ballast tanks when it wants to dive deep underwater?
options: Adding water increases the submarine's total weight so it exceeds the buoyant force, allowing it to sink
Water turns on the submarine's magnets
questions.explanation: To dive, ballast tanks fill with seawater (weight > upthrust); to resurface, compressed air blows water out (upthrust > weight).

questions.question: Match the force with its correct example: (i) Cricket ball stopping on its own — (ii) Compass needle pointing North — (iii) Fruit falling from a tree.
options: (i) Frictional force — (ii) Magnetic force — (iii) Gravitational force
(i) Magnetic force — (ii) Electrostatic force — (iii) Muscular force
questions.explanation: A rolling ball stops due to friction, a compass aligns via magnetic force, and a fruit falls due to gravity.

questions.question: Find the ODD one out based on contact vs non-contact nature of force:
questions.explanation: Gravitational, magnetic, and electrostatic forces are non-contact forces, whereas friction is a contact force.

questions.question: Find the ODD one out based on SI units:
questions.explanation: newton, dyne, and kgf are all units of force/weight, whereas kilogram is the unit of mass.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A person's weight on the Moon is only about one-sixth of their weight on Earth.
Reason (R): The Moon's gravitational pull is about one-sixth that of the Earth, though the person's mass stays the same.
options: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Weight equals mass × local gravity; because lunar gravity is ~1/6th of Earth's while mass is constant, weight becomes ~1/6th.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Pumice rock can float on the surface of water.
Reason (R): Pumice contains numerous trapped air pockets formed during rapid cooling of frothy lava, making its overall density less than that of water.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.explanation: Trapped gas bubbles make pumice porous and lighter than an equal volume of water, enabling it to float.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Two balloons rubbed with a woollen cloth repel each other when hung side by side.
Reason (R): Both balloons acquire opposite kinds of electrical charges upon rubbing.
options: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.explanation: The two balloons repel because they acquire the SAME (like) kind of charge when rubbed identically with wool — opposite charges would attract!

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Aeroplanes and racing boats are given smooth, pointed streamlined bodies.
Reason (R): Streamlining increases fluid friction so the vehicle grips the air and water better.
options: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Streamlining is specifically designed to REDUCE (not increase) fluid friction/drag in air and water.

questions.question: State which of the following statements is TRUE:
options: Due to friction, the speed of a rolling ball on flat ground increases
A force is always required to change the speed or direction of motion of an object
Weight is measured in kilograms in the SI system
There is no force between two charged objects placed slightly apart
questions.explanation: Any change in speed or direction requires an unbalanced force; friction slows balls down, charges interact at a distance, and weight is in newtons.

questions.question: A wooden cube of weight 15 N floats peacefully on the surface of a pond. What is the exact magnitude and direction of the buoyant force acting on the wooden cube?
questions.explanation: Because the cube is floating at rest (in equilibrium), the upward buoyant force must exactly equal its downward weight: 15 N upward.
